title: Soft 17 Rules in Canada: H17 vs S17 Blackjack
excerpt: Does the dealer hit or stand on soft 17? This small blackjack rule changes the house edge. Here is how to spot it and what it means for Canadian players.
author: Lisa Davids
bodyHtml:
Blackjack looks the same from table to table, but small rule differences can change how much the game costs you. One of the most important is what the dealer does with a soft 17 in blackjack. Some tables have the dealer stand on all 17s, abbreviated S17, and others have the dealer hit a soft 17, abbreviated H17. This guide explains the difference, why it matters, and how Canadian players can check the rule before they sit down.

What is a soft 17?

A soft hand is any hand that contains an ace counted as eleven. A soft 17 is therefore an ace and a six, or an ace with several small cards that add up to the same total. It is called soft because the dealer cannot bust by taking one more card; the ace can drop to one and the hand becomes a hard total. A hard 17, such as ten plus seven, has no such flexibility.

Dealers follow fixed rules, so they have no decisions to make. At an S17 table, the dealer stands on every 17, soft or hard. At an H17 table, the dealer hits soft 17 but stands on hard 17. That one change gives the dealer extra chances to improve a hand that would otherwise sit at a weak total.

Why H17 costs players more

When the dealer hits soft 17, the dealer wins slightly more often. Because the ace cannot cause a bust on the next card, the dealer can only improve or stay about the same. Over many hands, that adds up to a higher house edge. The usual estimate is that H17 adds roughly a fifth of a percentage point to the house edge, assuming other rules are equal. That sounds tiny, but it applies to every hand you play, so it matters for anyone who plays for a long session.

To put it in practical terms, the cost of any rule difference shows up as extra money lost per hundred dollars wagered over the long run. It does not affect any single session in a predictable way, because blackjack remains a game of short-term variance. You can lose at a great table and win at a poor one. But over time, the better rules cost you less.

Other rules that interact with soft 17

The dealer's soft 17 rule is only one of several that determine how favourable a game is. Check these at the same time:

  • Blackjack payout. A 3 to 2 payout is standard. A 6 to 5 payout is much worse for players and should usually be avoided.
  • Number of decks. Fewer decks slightly favour the player, all else equal.
  • Doubling rules. Doubling on any two cards, and after splitting, helps the player.
  • Surrender. Late surrender is valuable, and our guide to early and late surrender explains when to use it.
  • Resplitting aces. Being allowed to resplit aces adds a little value.

An S17 table with a 6 to 5 payout can be far worse than an H17 table with 3 to 2. Always weigh the whole rule set, not a single item. Our broader look at which blackjack rules pay best compares the common combinations.

How to find the rule at an online casino

Reputable online casinos publish blackjack rules in the game information panel, which you can usually open from a menu or help icon inside the game. Look for wording such as "dealer stands on all 17s" or "dealer hits soft 17." The table layout itself sometimes prints the rule across the felt. If you cannot find it, check the provider's game rules page or ask live chat support.

Live dealer versus RNG

The rule can differ between the digital version and the live dealer version of the same casino's blackjack. Do not assume one matches the other. For a full comparison of those formats, read our guide to live blackjack versus RNG blackjack. You can also browse our blackjack game guide for the fundamentals.

Does basic strategy change?

Yes, slightly. Basic strategy is the set of mathematically best plays for every hand and dealer upcard. A few decisions differ between S17 and H17 tables. For example, some double-down and surrender plays change against a dealer ten or ace, and a couple of hands such as eleven versus an ace shift. If you rely on a strategy chart, make sure it matches the rule you are playing. Many charts come in both versions, and using the wrong one adds a small, avoidable cost.

Learning basic strategy is the single best thing you can do to reduce the house edge. Memorizing the full chart takes time, but most players can learn the core of it in a few sessions of practice with free play, where a casino offers it.

What soft 17 does not change

It is worth being clear about what a good rule set cannot do. No rule variation turns blackjack into a winning game for the average player, and no betting system overcomes the house edge. Increasing your bet after a loss does not change the odds. If you want to understand why, our article on the gambler's fallacy explains how streaks mislead.

Likewise, a favourable rule set will not protect you from a bad session. Variance in blackjack is high, and you can lose many hands in a row at even the best tables. Set a budget before you play and stick to it.

A simple table-selection routine

Before you sit down at a table, take thirty seconds to run this routine:

  • Open the rules panel and confirm S17 or H17.
  • Confirm the blackjack payout is 3 to 2.
  • Check doubling, splitting and surrender options.
  • Check the minimum and maximum bets against your bankroll.
  • Decide on a stop limit and a time limit before you begin.

If you are choosing between casinos, look at the table rules as one factor next to licensing, payments and support. Our casino hub and reviews section make comparison easier.

The bottom line

S17 is better for the player than H17, but the difference is small compared with the payout rule, which matters far more. Treat soft 17 as one of several checks, learn basic strategy for the version you play, and keep blackjack in its proper place: a form of entertainment with a built-in cost, not a source of income.
